chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: What State Street and Chicago clubs were like; mixed audiences
summary: Briggs describes the Deluxe as a large smoky dive on State Street, is unsure if audiences were mixed, compares New York's mixed clubs, and calls the Cotton Club a business proposition.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, let's stay. The Deluxe Cabaret, what did it look like? Was it a small place or was it --
It was pretty large. Pretty large, but to me it was a dive, like all the other dives with smoke and liquor and everything, as I was telling you.
But that was on State --
Yes, on State Street.
Do you know Chicago very well? Not well, but roughly.
Well, you can imagine what State Street was. It doesn't exist anymore. That's what a friend of mine, Roy Butler, from Chicago, he wrote and told me, he said, "You wouldn't know Chicago."
Briggs
Because it's all changed.
I've been invited with my wife and family to -- the person I gave you his name before, Warren Plath.
Right.
I've been invited to spend a vacation with them. We haven't decided yet, because my daughter hasn't finished her studies, you see.
Right.
And that's my main point, in life, to do something for my daughter and my wife before I go, because I'm -- you know my age. (Laughter).
Yes, I do. Well, it doesn't look like it's going to be just yet.
One can never tell.
Well, these clubs like the Deluxe, were these black and tans, or were these black clubs or white audiences or
Briggs
No, no, I couldn't tell you, 'cause I didn't pay that much attention.
Yeh.
I didn't stay that long. But it seems as though they were mixed.
Mixed?
Yes, we had in New York, you had Baron Wilkens.
That was mixed, was it?

That was mixed. In those days it was not as I found it when I went back in '74. That's why as I told you yesterday, the happenings, being mugged and everything else, is one of the reasons why I stay away. Not against anything else but that, just the mentality.
Right.
'Cause you had the
Briggs

-- you had all the clubs, the Cotton Club, I think, was the only one, that was a business proposition. That's what they said, I don't know. It was a business proposition. It just catered to Caucasians. But you see, even if that was the point, it's a business proposition. That's the way I look at it. It's a business proposition. In all this business, you have to be broad-minded in life, if you want to get anywhere. Or live together with everyone. You must be broadminded.
